name: World-Building and Continuity
title: World-Building and Continuity
answer: World-building and continuity is the craft of making a fictional setting feel coherent across many works and many hands. It covers geography, history, languages, magic or technology rules, social structures, timelines, character backstories, and the small details that readers notice when they break. In AI-assisted writing, the scope expands to include prompt libraries, style guides, and retrieval systems that keep generated text aligned with an established canon. The site's glossary, which currently lists 686 terms, is one example of the controlled vocabulary that supports this work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: World-building and continuity work runs on documents, databases, and version control as much as on imagination. A typical setup includes a story bible, a timeline, a character registry, a place gazetteer, and a ruleset for how the world works. AI tools add searchable lore databases and retrieval systems that feed relevant passages into a prompt. The site tracks 732 AI tools, and a subset of them can help with drafting, summarizing, and cross-checking continuity, but the core infrastructure remains the written canon.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with a canon document and a set of rules, then write, review, and reconcile new material against it. They use outlines, style sheets, wikis, and checklists to catch contradictions in names, dates, distances, and abilities. When AI is involved, the common method is to generate options, then have a human editor verify each detail against the source of truth. Some teams use automated consistency checks, such as searching for a character's eye color or a city's founding date across all drafts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: World-building and continuity raise questions about who owns the setting, the characters, and the derived works. Provenance matters because a generated detail may come from training data, a user prompt, or a human author, and that chain affects rights and credit. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 involving AI music services, which shows that these questions are being tested in practice. Teams often keep an audit trail of prompts, model versions, and edits so they can explain where a piece of canon came from.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward living story bibles that update as new works are published and as models improve at long-context recall. Expect more integration between writing environments and continuity databases, so a draft can flag a broken timeline before a human reads it. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, 1000 video models, and 2000 audio models, and as those media join text in transmedia worlds, continuity will need to span visuals, sound, and dialogue. The hard problem will remain the same, which is deciding what counts as canon when many tools and many authors can add to it.
